 Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,
closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 4:00 pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be
summarized by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City
Council and will also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be
recorded for public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

  11
 PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

  BACKGROUND:  The District  was established  in 1981 and operates  under  the Landscaping

 improvements,  such as landscaping  and street lighting.  Since the District  covers  the entire  City,
the assessment  is levied  on all properties  throughout  the City.

To remain  compliance  with  the rules of the district,  District  revenue  can only be used to maintain
and operate  landscaping  and lighting  systems  throughout  the  City  and on City  streets.  This
includes  expenses  for  landscaping  (trees,  shrubs,  grass,  irrigation,  and drainage)  and lighting
systems (streetlights,  decorative  fixtures,  traffic  signals,  and related  equipment),  including  labor
and materials.

Each  year,  the  District's  assessments  are levied  and  collected  by  the  Los  Angeles  County
Assessor's  Office  ("County")  on behalf  of the City  through  the property  tax roll.  In order  for the
County  to levy  and collect  the assessments,  the City  Council  must  take certain  actions  required
by the County  and in accordance  with  applicable  state law.  The  actions  presented  to the City
Council  are part  of the  annual  proceedings  necessary  to  authorize  the  County  to place  the
assessments  on the tax roll  and collect  them on behalf  of the City.

On  January  13,  2026,  the  City  Council  adopted  Resolution  No.  2026-01-CC  to  initiate
proceedings  for FY 2026/27  and directed  the preparation  of the Engineer's  Report.  On April  28,

An  Assessment  District  allows  the City  to charge  a fee (assessment)  to properties  that benefit
from  public  improvements,  such  as enhanced  landscaping  and  street  lighting.  These  public
improvements  are considered  a special  benefit  to adjacent  properties.  Funding  for maintenance
and services  comes  from  the annual  assessments  paid by property  owners  within  the District.  To
continue  collecting  these  assessments  for  FY  2026/27,  the  City  must  prepare  an Engineer's
Report  annually  and hold  a public  hearing,  as required  by the Landscaping  and Lighting  Act  of
1972.

   FREQUENTLY  ASKED  QUESTIONS

WHAT  IS A BID?
BID is an acronym  for "Business  Improvement  District"  and it is an additional  tax fee on property  within
a defined  geographic  boundary  in which the revenues  raised from this additional  tax fee are spent only
within  the same area.

I S TH IS A NE W TAX ?
No, the  City Council  adopted  the  BID on November  2, 1970.  This additional  tax fee  has been
renewed  every  year since  and the fee amounts  have  remained  the same.

WHEN  IS THE  ADDITIONAL  TAX  FEE DUE?
The additional  tax fee is due and payable  at the same time as the business license  renewal.

HOW  ARE  THE  ADDITIONAL  TAX  FEES  CALCULATED?
The additional tax fees are determined by the annual gross receipts and range between S15-S400. See
enclosed  fee schedule.

HOW  ARE  THE-ADDITIONAL  TAX  FEES  COLLECTED  USED?
The additional  tax fees collected  can be used for the following  purposes  only:
  1. ) Decoration  of any public  place in the area.
  2. ) Promotion  of public  events which  are to take place in public  places in the area.
  3. ) The general  promotion  of retail trade  activities  in the area.

W H0  M AN AGE S THE  BID?
The BID is managed  by the Tweedy  Mile Advisory  Board. The Board is appointed  by the City Council
and serves in an advisory  capacity  by submitting  request  for their  approval  on expenditures  of revenues
collected  from the additional  tax.

WHEN  DOES  THE  BOARD  MEET?
The Tweedy  Mile Advisory  Board meets  monthly  on the first  Monday  of the month  at 6:00 p.m at the
City Hall Council  Chambers.  The meetings  are open to the public  and the agendas  are posted  on  the
city's website  at www.cityofsouthzate.org

HOW  D O I PR OTE ST ?
A Public Hearing has been scheduled  for the City Council to hear oral and written  comments.  A business
owner  can attend  the  public  hearing  and  simply  state  verbally  that  they  protest  the  levy of the
additional  tax fees. A written  protest  can also be submitted  and must contain  the business  owner's
name and business  address.  Written  protests  against the proposed  additional  tax fees shall be mailed
or delivered  to the City Clerk's Office,  8650 California  Avenue,  South Gate, California,  90280 or emailed
to yglaze@so@ate.or@  no later than 5:00 p.m., on May 26, 2026.

At the end of the Public Hearing,  the City Council  shall determine  whether  sufficient  protests  equaling
50 percent  or more of the additional  tax fees proposed  have been received.  If sufficient  protests  are

received,  the additional  tax fees shall not be approved.

Honorable  Mayor  and City Council:

It is my honor to present the City of South Gate's Proposed  Budget for Fiscal Year (FY)
2026-27.  This budget is the City's financial plan and operating  blueprint  for the year
ahead. It was prepared with two linked objectives:  protecting  the core municipal  services
residents  depend on and moving the City toward long-term  fiscal resilience  in a difficult
fiscal environment.

The FY 2026-27 Proposed  Budget totals $228.3 million in appropriations  across all funds,
departments,  and affiliated  entities, including the South Gate Housing Authority  and the
Successor  Agency  to the Community  Development  Commission.  The General  Fund,
which  supports  core  services  such  as police,  parks,  public  works,  community
development,  and administrative  operations,  includes  $72.2  million  in expenditures
against $68.2  million in projected  revenues.

This budget  is technically  balanced,  but it is not structurally  balanced.  Recurring
expenditures  continue to exceed recurring revenues. The remaining  gap is closed through
the one-time use of $2.25 million  from the Budget Stabilization  Reserve  and a modest
drawdown  of unassigned  General Fund balance. These tools are appropriate  to manage
a transition year, but they are not permanent  solutions.  To put it simply, the City needs to
b ring in substantial  new revenue or make permanent  cuts to City services to reduce the
level of response the Community  has enjoyed in the past.

Over  the  last  two  budget  cycles,  the  City  has  taken  substantial  corrective  action.
Departments  identified approximately  $2.0 million in General Fund reductions  in FY 2025-
26 and an additional  $7.3 million in FY 2026-27.  These reductions,  taken together,  close
most oT the $11.3 million planning gap originally  identified for FY 2026-27 and described
to the City Council during the budget study sessions. The remaining  gap is closed through
the one-time use of reserves.

For several years, the City relied on more than $18 million in one-time American  Rescue
Plan Act (ARPA) funds to offset ongoing  operating  costs. Those federal funds helped
maintain services during and after the pandemic,  but they were temporary.  With ARPA
now largely  expended,  the City must  rely on recurring  local revenues,  ongoing

expenditure controls,  or both to support ongoing services.  Restoring  structural  balance
remains the City's central fiscal task over the next 24 months.

Budget  Conditions  and Fiscal  Pressures

The FY 2024-25  Annual Comprehensive  Financial  Report (ACFR) provides  important
context. The City ended the year with positive fund balances  and an increase in overall
net position,  which shows continued  fiscal discipline  and the City's ability to meet its
financial  obligations.  At the same time, the ACFR makes clear that strong year-end
financial  statements  do not, by themselves,  mean the operating  budget is structurally
balanced. The structural  issue is not whether the City can pay its bills today. The issue is
whether recurring revenues are sufficient to support recurring services over time.

The City's operating  pressure  is driven by a combination  of expired one-time  funding,
revenue  soffness,  inflation,  and mandated  or market-driven  cost growth.  The most
significant  cost pressures  since FY 2019-20 are:
  *  CalPERS  Unfunded  Accrued  Liability  (UAL)  payments  grew  from  approximately
  $6.0 million  in FY 2019-20  to $11.1 million in FY 2026-27,  an increase  of about  85
  percent.
  *  Healthandancillarybenefitcostsincreasedfromapproximately$5.0millionto$7.1

In total, these factors have added roughly  $11.5 million in annual recurring  cost pressure
since FY 2019-20,  including the ongoing  Street Lighting and Landscaping  subsidy.  For
FY 2026-27  alone,  the City is absorbing  approximately  $4.1 million  in new or incremental
pressure,  including  lower revenue  projections  of about $2.7 million,  $0.6 million in
additional  UAL costs, $0.5 million in insurance  growth, and $0.3 million in election costs.

The $7.3 million in proposed  reductions  for FY 2026-27,  in addition to the $2.0 million
reduced in FY 2025-26, are spread across every department  and include both operational
efficiencies  and service-level  reductions.  The Citywide impact includes a net reduction of
32 full time authorized  positions through targeted  position eliminations.  This includes 13
positions  in the Police Department  alone, as well as reductions  in training,  equipment,
and contracted  services.  These measures  will affect service delivery:  residents  should
expect  longer  wait times  at public  counters,  slower  departmental  response  and
processing  times, reduced capacity  in homelessness  and public health response,  and
diminished  financial flexibility to respond to unforeseen  events.

General  Fund  Overview

The General Fund is the City's largest and most flexible fund. It supports Police,  Parks
and Recreation,  Public Works,  Community  Development,  Engineering,  Code
Enforcement,  Facilities, and core administrative  functions.  Major General  Fund
department appropriations for FY 2026-27 include:
  *  Police: $41.9 million
  *  ParksandRecreation:$lO.7million
  @ Public Works (General Fund portion): $6.2 million

  *  Community Development (General Fund portion): $5.6 million

General Fund revenues were originally projected at $70.9 million, but updated estimates
now total $68.2 million. This  is approximately  $2.7 million  below  earlier planning
assumptions and about I % below the FY 2025-26 year-end  projection of $68.9 million.
The  primary  drivers  are softness  in State  Sales  Tax,  the local  I percent  transactions  and
use tax  (Measure  P), and  user  fee  revenues.  Revenue  projections  are  based  on trend
analysis,  professional  judgment,  and  estimates  from  outside  agencies  and  consultants,
including  HdL Companies  for sales  and property  tax.

The Proposed Budget includes the use of $2.25 million from the Budget Stabilization
Reserve and $2.83 million in General Fund transfers out. Affer all budgeted activities, the
City projects:
  *  Year-end unassigned General Fund balance of $3.0 million.
  *  Budget Stabilization Reserve reduced from $3.77 million to $1.52 million.
  *  Emergency Reserve maintained at $13.0 million (consistent with adopted reserve
  policy).
  *  PERS/OPEB  Reserve maintained  at $1.73 million.

Transfers  between  funds  are  a  routine  and  necessary  budgeting  tool.  They  direct
restricted  or prior-year  resources  to eligible  uses  in the  budget  year.  At the  same  time,
restricted  funds  cannot  be used  to solve  unrestricted  General  Fund  operating  deficits
unless  the  expense  is legally  eligible  for that  funding  source.  This  is why  the  City  may
have  significant  activity  in capital,  grant,  enterprise,  or special  revenue  funds  while  still
facing  pressure  in the General  Fund.

Capital  Improvement  Program  (CIP)

The  FY 2026-27  Capital Improvement  Program  includes  $19.7 million  in new
appropriations across 32 active projects. Most CIP funding  comes from restricted  special
revenues,  state  and federal  grants,  and  enterprise  funds.  These  funds  are important  for
infrastructure,  but  they  are  generally  not  available  to support  General  Fund  operating
services.

The CIP advances  several  critical  priorities,  including:
  *  Street  rehabilitation  and  complete-streets  improvements  funded  by sources  such
  as SB 1, Measure  R, Measure  M, Proposition  A, Proposition  C, and  Gas Tax.

The direct General  Fund contribution  to the CIP is limited to $378,000.  This approach
allows the City to continue infrastructure  investment while protecting scarce discretionary

Master  Fee Schedule  and Cost  Recovery

The Proposed  Master Fee Schedule  includes cost-recovery  updates across departments,
including  many fee adjustments  of approximately  7 percent,  and selected  actual-cost
recovery  provisions  for outside consultant  or staff costs that vary by project. This is an
important fiscal management  step because fees should be reviewed regularly and, where
legally allowed, aligned with the cost of providing the service.

Fee updates  alone will not close the structural  General  Fund gap. Many municipal
services  are not fee-supported,  and fee revenue must comply with legal cost-recovery
limits. Still, the proposed schedule helps reduce unnecessary  General Fund subsidies for
services that benefit specific users, improve fairness among taxpayers  and fee payers,
and support a broader cost-recovery  study in the near future.

Service-Level  Impacts

The reductions  proposed for FY 2026-27 affect every department.  The impacts are most
visible  in Police,  Parks and Recreation,  Public  Works,  Community  Development,
Administrative  Services,  and Human  Resources  because  these departments  provide
most of the City's direct public-facing and operationaJ support services.

Examples  of service impacts include reduced sworn and civilian public safety capacity,
elimination  or reduction  of several Police support programs,  fewer records staff hours,
longer investigations,  elimination  of the crossing guard program at the close of FY 2025-
26, with the City coordinating  with the Los Angeles  Unified School District and local
schools on transition  options, the closure of our community  pool and sports fields for the
winter months, reduced administrative  and finance processing  capacity, less specialized
risk management  oversight,  longer maintenance  cycles, and reduced capacity to support
capital project delivery and public counter activity. These impacts are real, and they reflect
the service trade-off required when recurring revenues are insufficient  to support existing
service levels.

Fiscal  Outlook  and  Structural  Imbalance

The  FY 2026-27  Proposed  Budget  reduces  the structural  deficit,  but it does  not eliminate
it. Corrective  action  will still be needed  in the next budget  cycle.  The City's  options  remain
the same:  sustainable  new  revenue,  further  ongoing  expenditure  reductions,  or  a
combination  of both.

Absent  additional  corrective  measures,  the  City  projects  a recurring  General  Fund
shortfall  in the range  of $4 million  to $5 million  in FY 2027-28  before  any revenue
modernization  or program  restoration  is considered.  Two factors will shape  that Forecast:
  @  The  City's  2005  Police  Pension  Obligation  Bond  is scheduled  to be paid  off in FY
  2027-28,  eliminating approximately $2.0 million  in annual  debt service.
  *  Continued  growth  in  CalPERS  UAL  payments,  insurance  premiums,  labor,
  maintenance,  and other  operating  costs  will offset  a substantial  portion  of that relief
  unless  paired  with  revenue  or expenditure  action.

The  principal  recurring  drivers  of cost  growth  remain:
  *  Growing  CalPERS  UAL  amortization  obligations
  @  Health  and  liability  insurance  premium  growth
  *  Increasing  excess  liability  coverage  costs
  @  Continuing  General  Fund  subsidy  to the Street  Lighting  & Landscaping  District
  *  Deferred  maintenance  and unfunded  capital  requirements  across  the City's  aging
  infrastructure  and assets

The  core  fiscal  issue  is alignment.  The  City  must  align  recurring  revenues  with  recurring
obligations  while  preserving  reserves,  protecting  essential  services,  and  continuing  to
invest  in infrastructure.  Structural  balance  is achievable,  but  it will require  sustained
discipline  and clear  policy  direction.

Strategic  Initiatives  Undenuay

To address  the structural  imbalance  and the service-level  pressures  it creates,  the City is
advancing  several  initiatives:
  *  Master  Fee Schedule  and  Cost  Allocation  Study:  Update  fees  and  cost  allocation
  methods  so  legally  recoverable  services  are  charged  appropriately  and
  transparently.
  *  Revenue  Modernization:  Prepare  a potential  November  2026  Utility  Users  Tax
  (UUT)  measure  on the ballot  for voter  consideration.
  *  Economic  Development:  Focus  on  attracting  tax-generating  businesses,
  supporting  existing  local  businesses,  and  revitalizing  underutilized  commercial
  corridors.
  *  Internal  Controls  and  Administrative  Modernization:  Continue  strengthening
  procurement,  contract  governance,  banking,  investment  management,  technology
  systems,  and financial  reporting  practices.

 BACKGROUND:  Illegal  dumping  continues  to be a widespread  issue throughout  the City,
particularly  along  public  rights-of-way,  alleys,  and vacant  areas. A recurring  component  of this
activity  is  the  disposal  of  waste  tires,  which  contributes  to  visual  blight  and  creates
environmental  and public  health  concerns.  Accumulated  tires can attract  pests, serve as breeding
grounds  for mosquitoes,  and pose fire risks if not addressed  promptly.

The City  currently  relies  on limited  operational  funds  to address  illegal  dumping  on an ongoing
basis. With  existing  fiscal  constraints,  these cleanup  efforts  place continued  pressure  on available
resources.

In addition  to the direct  costs  of removal,  illegal  dumping  diverts  staff  time  and operational
resources  away  from  other  critical  maintenance  activities.  Crews  must  routinely  respond  to
complaints,  inspect  sites, and coordinate  cleanups,  which  can delay  scheduled  work  and reduce
overall  service  efficiency.  As  dumping  continues  to  occur,  these  impacts  are  ongoing  and
compound  over time.

The CalRecycle  Waste  Tire  Cleanup  Grant  Program  provides  a funding  opportunity  to directly
support  these  efforts  by  covering  the  costs  associated  with  the  collection,  removal,
transportation,  recycling,  and disposal  of waste tires.  Securing  this grant would  allow  the City  to
expand  cleanup  activities,  reduce  the burden  on existing  resources,  and address  illegal  dumping
more  efficiently  without  additional  impact  to the General  Fund.

   Although  the original  contract  does not  include  formal  extension  provisions,  the City  Council

  PROJECT N0. 732-ARC

  PURPOSF,:  To approve a professional services agreement with NV5, Inc, ("NV5")  to perform
  construction management and inspection services for the City Hall Reroof Project.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTTONS:  The City Council will consider:
  a. Appro'ving  an Agreement  with  NV5,  Inc. to perform  construction  management and
  inspectionservices011the City Hall ReroofCity ProjectNo. 732-ARC(Reroof Pro3ect),
  in an amount not-to-exceed $85,011;
  b.  Authorizing the City Manager to approve and execute amendments to the Agreement up
  to a cumulative atnount of $50,000 and;
  c.  Authorizing the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form acceptable to the City
  Attorriey.

  FISCAL n%4PACT:The proposed Agreement is for an amount not to exceed $85,011, and it
  will be funded by Building and Infrastucture Maintenance (BIM) Funds budgeted in the
  FY25/26 Capital Improvement Prog;ram.

  ANALYSIS:  Conmuction  of this project requires o'ver 500 hours of management  and
  inspection effort. The Department of Public Works, Engineering Division, lacks sufficient in-
  house staff to perform these taslcs. Therefore, it is recommended to retain a constnuction
  maiiagement and inspection services consultant to oversee the work.

  Staff issued a Request for Task Proposals ("RFTP") to the fo'ir As-Needed Engineering Firms
  and received two proposals. NV5 was determined to be the highest qualified to provide the
  services requested. NV5os initial cost proposal was the second lowest, but after negotiations,
  their proposal became comparable to the lowest fee proposal.

  BACKGROUND:  The existing City Hail roof is in a state of disrepair and has experienced
  multiple leaks during rain events, adversely impacting City operations and creating the potential
  for further interior damage if not addressed. To address these issues, the City is in the process of
  implementing the City Hall Reroof Project. The Project includes tbe removal and replacement of
  the existing roof system, including the concrete roof tiles, underlayment, and wood battens. The

 improvements  will  help protect  the building  from  future  water  intrusion,  extend  the useful  life of
the facility,  and reduce  ongoing  maintenance  and repair  needs.

The design  phase has been completed,  and construction  bids have been received  thus the project
is now  ready  for construction.  Construction  is anticipated  to begin  in July  2026  and take  49
calendar  days to complete.  Construction  management  and inspection  services  are needed  to
administer  and inspect  construction  activities.

On  March  18,  2026,  a RFTP  was  issued  to the four  (4) prequalified  as needed  engineering

  Consultant  Fee Proposal  Negotiated  Proposal

  Interwest  $85,240

A  selection  committee  consisting  of the  City's  Associate  Engineer  and  Water  Resources  &
Development  Division  Manager,  evaluated  the proposals.  All  consultants  met the qualifications
criteria  which  included  construction  manager,  inspector  experience,  and  labor  compliance.
However,  NV5's  staff demonstrated  experience  on projects  similar  in scope to this project  and  is

therefore  recommended  for the contract.

NV5  provides  the following  benefits  to the project:

  *  Competitive  Fees - The fee proposal  is $85,011  and is competitive,  as it represents  the
  lowest  proposal  received  from  the RFTP.

  @  Experienced  Construction  Manager  - The Construction  Manager  has over  30 years  of
  experience.

  @  Qualified  Staff  -  NV5  offers  a qualified  team  with  experience,  knowledge,  and
  professionalism  for the Project.  NV5  has licensed  engineers,  construction  and program
  managers,  inspectors,  office  engineers,  technicians,  and administrative  support  to manage
  the Project.

  *  Qualified  Team  - NV5's  in-house  team  will  provide  special  inspections,  if necessary,
  testing  and  labor  compliance.  The  inspector  and the alternate  inspector  have  over  30
  years  of experience  in the industi'y,  which  provides  the ability  to ensure  the Project  is
  constructed  in accordance  with  the plans and specifications.

  *  Similar  Projects  - NV5's  core specialties  are construction  management  and inspection
  of Public  Works  projects.  NV5  recently  completed  numerous  projects  of similar  scope.
  Similar  project  has been successfully  completed  in the past for the City  of South  Gate.

The  scope  of  services  in  the  proposed  Agreement  consists  of  construction  management,
construction  inspection,  and labor compliance.

  ESTIMATES  FOR THE SOUTHEAST  GATF,WAY  ACCESS I1%4PROVF,MENTS
  PROJECT, CITY PROJECT N0. 715-ST., FEDERAL PROJECT NO. ATPL-5257(044)
  AND 5257(046)

  PURPOSE:  To award a Professional Services Agreement to AYCE Consulting Engineers, Inc.
  (AYCE) for engineering design services to prepare Plans, Specifications, and Estimates for the
  Southeast Gateway Access Improvements Project ("Project").

  RECOMMENDED  ACTTONS: The City Council will consider;
  a, Approving an agreement with AYCE Consulting Engineers, Inc. to provide engineering
  services ("Agreement") to prepare Plans, Specifications, and Estimates for the Southeast
  Gateway Access Improvements Project, City Project No. 715-ST, in an amount not-to-
  exceed $247,923;
  b. Authorizing the City Manager to approve and execute amendments up to a cumulative
  amount of $50,000; and
  c. AuthorizingtheMayortoexecutetheAgreementinaformacceptabletotheCityAttorney.

  FISCAL IMPACT:  There is no fiscal impact to the General Fund. The proposed Agreement is
  in the amount of $247,923 and will be funded with Propositi6n C Funds budgeted for the Project
  in the FY 2025/27 Capital Improvement Program.

  ANALYSJS: To procure the proposed contract, the City issued a Request for Proposals for
  engineering services to prepare Plans, Specifications, and Estinnates (PS&E) for the Project. The
  consultant selection process included review of written proposals and interviews in accordance
  with the City's procurement process and applicable federal/local assistance requirements.
  Following the evaluation of the proposals and interviews, AYCE Consulting Engineers, Inc. was
  identified as the top-ranked consultant. City staff then entered into negotiations with AYCE to
  refine the scope of work and fee. Based on those negotiations, AYCE submitted a revised fee
  proposal dated April 23, 2026, in the amount of $247,923. Staff have reviewed the negotiated
  scope and fee and determined that the proposal is reasonable for the level of effort required to
  deli'ver the project through final PS&E, federal a'uthorization support, bidding assistance, and

  219
 limited  construction  support.  As such, AYCE  is recommended  for the contract.

The project  is funded  with  Federal  Active  Transportation  Program  'funds  for  construction  and
Proposition  C Local  Return  funds  for design.  Because  construction  will  include  federal  funding,
the design  phase  must  be advanced  in accordance  with  applicable  Caltrans  Local  Assistance
Procedures  Manual  requirements,  including  preparation  of the E-76  construction  authorization
package.

BACKGROUND:  The Southeast  Gateway  Access  Improvements  Project  will  improve  first/last-
mile access, pedestrian  safety,  bicycle  connectivity,  ADA  accessibility,  and roadway  conditions  in
the Hollydale  area and along corridors  serving  future  Southeast  Gateway  Line  stations.  The project
includes  a combination  of active  transportation  and roadway  improvements,  including  Class  II
bicycle  lanes,  Class  III  bicycle  routes  with  shared  lane  markings,  high-visibility  crosswalks,
Rectangular  Rapid  Flashing  Beacons,  raised  medians,  street  lighting,  sidewalk  and ADA  curb
ramp upgrades,  roadway  resurfacing  prior  to final  striping,  and improved  connectivity  to the Los
Angeles  River  Bike  Path.

On February  6, 2026,  the Request  for Proposals  was released  electronically  through  PlanetBids,
published  on the  City's  website,  and advertised  in trade journals.  On March  5, 2026,  six  (6)
proposals  from  prospective  consultants  were submitted  to the City  Clerk's  Office.

A three-member  selection  panel,  consisting  of the City's  Transportation  and Capital  Improvement
Program  Division  Manager,  the  City's  Senior  Civil  Engineer,  and  the  City  of  Downey's
Superintendent,  reviewed  the proposals  and interviewed  three  consulting  firms.  The  selection
process  was conducted  as a qualifications-based  selection  process  and considered  several  factors,
including  the qualifications  of the proposed  project  manager  and project  team,  experience  on
similar  projects,  understanding  of the project  scope  and technical  issues,  and overall  project
approach.  Based on the evaluation  criteria,  AYCE  Consulting  Engineers,  Inc. received  the highest
ranking  from  the panel.

AYCE  Consulting  Engineers,  Inc. provides  the following  benefits  to the Project:

  *  Experienced  Consulting  Firm  -  AYCE  is  a professional  civil  engineering  firm
  established  in 2015 and based in Santa Ana, California.  AYCE  specializes  in street design,
  transportation  engineering,  municipal  street  improvements,  roadway  and  intersection
  improvements,  ADA  accessibility  upgrades,  active  transportation  facilities,  utility
  coordination,  and  corridor  modernization.  AYCE  has  successfully  delivered  similar
  projects  for public  agencies  including  the City of Carson,  City of Costa Mesa, City  of Long
  Beach,  City  of Santa Aria,  City  of Los Angeles,  Caltrans  District  7, LA  Metro,  OCTA,
  LAWA,  and LA  County.

  Qualified  Staff  - The proposed  Project  Manager,  is a registered  Civil  Engineer  with  more
  than  37 years  of  experience  in  transportation  infrastructure.  His  experience  includes
  multimodal  corridor  improvements,  roadway  rehabilitation,  ADA-compliant  pedestrian
  upgrades,  pavement  design,  PS&E  preparation,  interagency  coordination,  federal  funding
  compliance,  Caltrans  coordination,  and construction-phase  support.  The project  team also
  includes  Lead  Project  Engineer,  who  has extensive  experience  in roadway  resurfacing,

  220
   pavement  rehabilitation,  ADA  compliance,  pedestrian  safety  improvements,  and multi-
  agency  coordination.

  Negotiated  Competitive  Fee - AYCE  submitted  an original  fee proposal  of $293,462,
  which  was negotiated  to $247,923. The negotiated  fee includes  1,140  AYCE  staff hours,
  field  survey  services,  landscape  architecture  support,  E-76  construction  authorization
  support,  bidding  assistance,  and limited  construction  support  for  the six-month  design
  schedule.

AYCE's  scope  of services  includes  project  management,  agency  and utility  coordination,  field
survey,  permit  coordination,  preparation  of specifications  and cost estimates,  engineering  design
drawings,  preparation  of the E-76  package  for construction  authorization,  bidding  support,  pre-
construction  and job-site  meeting  support,  responses  to RFIs and submittals,  and as-built  drawings.

The design  phase will  begin  in June 2026,  and take five (5) months  to complete.

  PURPOSE:  To award a construction  inanagement  and inspection  service  agreement  for the I-
  710 Firestone  Boulevard  Southbound  On-Ramp  and Firestone  Boulevard  Street Improvement
  Project  ("On  Ramp Project").  The project  is scheduled  to start constnuction  in Fall 2026.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council  will  consider:
  a.  Approving  aii  agreement  with  FCG  Consultants,  Inc.,  to  provide  Construction
  Management  and Inspection  Services  ("Agreement=')  for the construction  of the I-710
  Firestone  Boulevard  Southbound  On-Ramp  and Firestone  Boulevard  Street Improvement
  Project,  City ProjectNo.  354-ST,  in an amount  not-to-exceed  $900,467;
  b.  Authorizing  the City  Manager  to approve  and execute  amendments  up to a cumulative
  amount  of $130,000;  and
  c,  Authorizing  the Mayor  to execute the Agreement  in a form acceptable  to the City Attorney.

  FJSCAL  ACT:  There is no fiscal impact  to the General  Fund. The proposed  agreetnent  is in
  the amount  of $900,467  and will  be funded  with  Metro  Measure  R Funds.

  ANALYSIS:  TheOn-RampProjectisincludedintheCapitalImprovementProgram,withdesign
  plans completed  and approved  by Caltrans  in September  2025. Construction  will  be advertised
  uponreceipt  ofthe  Caltrans E-76 authorization,  with construction  anticipatedto  begin in Fall 2026.
  Due to the scale and complexity  of the project,  the Depmtment  of Public  Works  Engineering
  Division  requires  a construction  management  services  consultant  to oversee  construction  and
  inspection,  as tl'ffls effort  exceeds  current  staff  capacity  and requires  specialized  expertise  in
  Caltrans  Standard  Plans and constuction  methods.  A Requestfor  Proposals  (RFP) was issued, and
  FCG  Consultants,  Inc.  was identified  as the highest-ranked  firm.  The  initial  fee proposal  of
  $1,035,154  was negotiated  down  to $900,467  to align  with  the project's  needs, and the final
  negot'ated  fee is considered  reasonable  and consistent  with  industy  standards  for constuction
  management  services.

 BACKGROUND:  The  Onramp  Project  is a high-priority  infrastructure  project  designed  to
improve  traffic  flow  and pedestrian  safety  at one of the City's  busiest  interchanges.  Due to the
technical  complexity  of the project,  including  Caltrans  coordination  and heavy  traffic  control
requirements,  the Public  Works  Department  requires  specialized  Construction  Management  (CM)
SerVlCeS.

On July  28, 2025, a RFP was released  electronically  through  Planetbids,  published  on the City's
website,  and  advertised  in trade  journals.  On  September  11,  2025,  five  (5) proposals  from
perspective  consultants  were  submitted  to the City  Clerk's  Office.  A panel  comprised  of three
members  (City  Transportation  and Capital  Improvement  Program  Division  Manager,  City  Senior
Engineer  and City  of Downey  Principal  Engineer)  reviewed  the proposals  and interviewed  all five
consulting  firms.  This  qualification-based  selection  process  weighed  several  factors  such  as
project  manager  and team  qualifications,  experience  on similar  projects  and understanding  of
technical  issues.  Based  on the criteria,  FCG  Consultants,  Inc. received  the highest  ranking  from
the panel.

FCG  Consultants,  Inc., provides  the following  benefits  to the Project:

  *  Experienced  Consulting  Firm  - FCG  Consultants,  Inc.  is a civil  engineering  firm
  established  in 2010 with  30 professional  employees.  FCG Consultants,  Inc.  specializes  in
  the provision  of construction  management  construction  inspection,  plan  review,  project
  management,  and other civil  engineering  services.  FCG Consultants,  Inc. has successfully
  delivered  similar  projects  for cities  such as Lake  Elsinore,  Moorpark  and Irwindale.

  *  Qualified  Staff  - The selected  constniction  manager  is a registered  Civil  Engineer  and
  Qualified  SWPPP  Practitioner.  He  has more  than  28 years  of  construction  industry
  experience  in  the  transportation  field  which  includes  work  associated  with  grade
  separations,  freeway  interchanges,  major  urban  arterial  improvements,  freeway
  replacement,  and capital  improvement  projects.  The construction  inspector  has 30 years
  of experience  as a Public  Works  Inspector  for a wide  range  of projects,  with  a significant
  amount  of public  works  construction  observation  and special  inspection  experience.

  *  Negotiated  Competitive  Fees - FCG  Consultants,  Inc. submitted  an original  fee proposal
  of $1,035,154  which  was negotiated  to $900,467  and includes  a total  of 4,554  hours  of
  service  for the 18-month  construction  schedule.

Construction  is plaru"ied to begin  in Fall of 2026 and be completed  in 16 months.

PROJECT UNDERSTANDING

The project involves removing the existing southbound on-ramp and constructing Cl new ramp to connect  with
the widened Fires+one Boulevard bridge. Additional work includes road paving, embankment  construction,
concrete work, excavation, upgrades to the irrigation system, landscaping within the Caltrans right-of-way, and
other  related  construction  activities.

The Firestone Boulevard Street Improvement component will cover the segment between Rayo Avenue  and
Garfield Avenue. This work includes cold milling and repaving the existing roadway, new striping, construction
or raised median islands with irrigation and landscaping, replacement of concrete sidewalks,  curbs, and
gutters, installation of new curb ramps, and various other associated improvements.

SCOPE OF SERVICES

G3 proposes to offer Quality Assurance technical consulting, inspection, materials sampling,  and  testing
services on an as-needed basis for various tasks including earthwork, subgrade, aggregate  base,  HMA,  LCB,
JPCP and  concrete  testing.

the Cost File (Attachment A) and Schedule of Fees (Attachment  C). All services, including technical consulting
and laboratory testing, will be billed in accordance with the approved  schedule  of fees.

This estimate is based on the limited information  currently available.  Any work exceeding  the estimated  scope
will be billed  on a time-and-expense  basis.

 ANALYSIS:  The Fiscal  Year 2024  State Homeland  Security  Program  (SHSP),  administered  by
the  U.S.  Department  of  Homeland  Security  through  the  California  Governor's  Office  of
Emergency  Services  (Cal OES),  provides  funding  to local jurisdictions  to enhance  capabilities  to
prevent,  protect  against,  respond  to, and recover  from  acts of terrorism,  foreign  or domestic.

As  part  of this  program,  the City  of  South  Gate  has been  allocated  $75,000  to support  law
enforcement  equipment  investments.  The approved  project  includes  the purchase  and installation
of five  (5) CCTV  cameras  categorized  under terrorism  incident  prevention  and security  systems.
The  implementation  of  CCTV  camera  systems  will  enhance  situational  awareness,  support
investigative  efforts,  and strengthen  the Department's  ability  to monitor  and respond  to potential
threats.  These  systems  directly  align  with  homeland  security  objectives  by improving  detection,
deterrence,  and response  capabilities  related  to public  safety  and critical  infrastructure  protection.
All  grant-:funded  activities  must comply  with  federal,  state, and local requirements,  including  Title
2 Code of Federal  Regulations  (CFR)  Part 200, the Homeland  Security  Grant  Program  Notice  of
Funding  Opportunity  (NOFO),  and Cal OES guidelines.

Additionally,  the  City  is required  to  submit  biannual  performance  reports,  maintain  proper
procurement  documentation,  and  ensure  that  all  equipment  purchases  meet  the  Authorized
Equipment  List  (AEL)  standards.  Failure  to  comply  with  grant  requirements  may  result  in
reduction,  suspension,  or termination  of funding.

BACKGROUND:  The U.S. Department  of Homeland  Security  through  the Office  of Grants  and
Training  has provided  financial  assistance  for the SHSP  directly  to the California  Governor's
Office  of Emergency  Services  (Cal OES)  for the 2024  SHSP,  FAIN  #037-00000,  Federal  Award
dated October  28, 2024, with  a performance  period  of September  1, 2024, to May  31, 2027.

Cal  OES  is providing  these  funds  to the County  of Los  Angeles  (D{JNS  #052238763)  as its
Subgrantee.  Cal  OES  is responsible  for  managing  and overseeing  SHSP  funds  distributed  to
municipal  jurisdictions  in Los Angeles  County.  This specific  financial  assistance  is being provided
to the South  Gate Police  Department  to address  communication  equipment,  training,  and other
needs, helping  build  effective  prevention  and protection  capabilities  to prevent,  respond  to, and
recover  from  threats  or acts of terrorism.

The County  of Los Angeles,  as a subgrantee,  has obtained  approval  of the 2024 SHSP grant from
Cal OES in the total  amount  of $8,300,952.00,  and the South  Gate Police  Department  has been
allocated  funds in the amount  of $75,000.

This  project  supports  regional  and  national  homeland  security  priorities  by  enhancing  law
enforcement  capabilities  in surveillance,  detection,  and prevention  of potential  threats.

  ST ATEMENT  ON THE DRUG-FREE  WORKPLACE

To complywith  the enactment  of Senate Bill 1120, (Chapter 1170, Statutes of 1990), which established  the
Drug-Free  Workplace  Act  of 1990,  the
  (your  agency)
accordingly  provides this statement  of compliance.

In order to maintain funding eligibility, state agencies, along with those in receipt of grant and contractual
awards, must certify that they provide drug-free workplaces and have issued drug-free workplace statements
to their employees [Section 8355(a) of the Government Coded. Consequently, in accordance with this directive,
this statement is issued to meet this requirement.

The  (youragency), an agency within the State of California  has adopted this
statement in compliance with legislation which addresses issues to avoid the dangers arising from drug and
alcohol abuse in the workplace. These dangers include death and injury to the employee, co-workers, or the
public resulting from accidents, dereliction of duty, poor judgment and carelessness.  Substance abuse also
results in lost productivity,  reduced efficiency, and increased absenteeism  by the substance abuser and
interferes with the job performance of employees who do not use illegal or unauthorized substances. [Section
8355(b) (1)]

California law prohibits the unlawful manufacture, dispensation, possession,  or illegal use of a controlled
substance. That prohibition extends to all places and includes the worksite  of California state employees.
[Section 8355(a)]

Employees convicted of a violation  of criminal drug statute, when the violation occurred at an employee's
worksite, shall report the conviction  to the granting and monitoring State agency upon conviction. [Section
8356(a)(1)(2)]

In the event of the unlawful manufacture, distribution, dispensation, possession or illegal use of a controlled
substance at a State worksite, the State may take disciplinary action pursuant to the law and/or require the
satisfactory completion of a drug abuse assistance or rehabilitation program. [Section 8355(b)(4)]

The Employee Assistance  Program (EAP) provides drug problem assessment  and referral to appropriate
counseling and rehabilitation services. The EAP is available to all agency employees. Procedures exist to
ensure the confidentiality or EAP records. Contact your personnel office for further information.

It is the intent of the  (youragency) to ensure by execution of this statement  of
compliance that each employee shall abide by the terms of this drug-free workplace statement. [Section
8355(c)]

10. Program  Overview,  Objectives,  and  Priorities

  a.  Overview
  The Fiscal  Year  (FY)  2024 Homeland  Security  Grant  Program  (HSGP)  is one of the
  three grant programs  that constihite  the DHS/FEMA  focus  on enhancing  the ability  of
  state, local,  tribal,  and territorial  governments,  as well  as nonprofits,  to prevent,
  protect  against,  and respond  to terrorist  attacks.  These  grant  programs  are part of a
  comprehensive  set of measures  authorized  by Congress  and implemented  by DHS  to
  help strengthen  the Nation's  communities  against  potential  tetrorist  attacks.

  In FY 2024,  there are three components  of the HSGP:

  1)  State Homeland  Security  Program  (SHSP):  SHSP  assists state, local,  tribal,
  and territorial  (SLTT)  efforts  to build,  sustain,  and deliver  the capabilities
  necessary  to prevent,  prepare  for, protect  against,  and respond  to acts of
  terrorxsm.

  2)  Urban  Area  Securhy  Initiative  (UASI):  UASI  assists high-threat,  high-density
  Urban  Area  efforts  to build,  sustain,  and deliver  the capabilities  necessary  to
  prevent,  prepare  for, protect  against,  and respond  to acts of terrorism.

  3)  Operatiorx  Stoiiegarden  (OPSG):  OPSG  supports  enhanced  cooperation  and
  coordination  among  Customs  and Border  Protection  (CBP),  United  States
  Border  Patrol  (USBP),  and federal,  state, local,  tribal,  and tei'ritorial  law
  enforcement  agencies  to improve  overall  border  security.  OPSG provides
  funding  to support  joint  efforts  to secrire the United  States'  borders  along
  routes  of ingress/egress  to and from  international  borders,  to include  travel
  corridors  in states bordering  Mexico  and Canada,  as well  as states and
  territories  with  international  water  borders.  SLTT  law enforcement  agencies
  ritilize  their inherent  law enforcement  authorities  to support  the border  security
  mission  and do not receive  any additional  authority  by participating  in OPSG.

  Finally,  for FY 2024,  DHS  is focused  on tlie criticality  of information  sharing  and
  collaboration  to building  a national  culture  of preparedness  and protecting  against
  terrorism  and other threats  to our national  security.  The threats  to our nation  have
  evolved  dwing  the past two decades.  We now  face continuous  cyber  threats  by
  sophisticated  actors,  threats  to soft targets  and crowded  places,  and threats  from
  domestic  violent  extremists,  who represent  one of the most persistent  threats  to the
  nationl.  Tlierefore,  for FY 2024,  DHS  has identified  six priority  areas (see Section
  A.lO.b)  related  to the most  serious  threats  to the nation,  as well  as required  minimum
  funding  allocations.

  For a full  list of SHSP  and UASI  recipients  and a breakdown  of OPSG  fiinding  by
  state for FY 2023,  please  refer  to Information  Bulletin  (IB)  490a.

  b.  Goals,  Objectives,  and  Priorities
  . The HSGP  will  fund  SLTT  efforts  and strengthen  capabilities  of SLTT
  governments  to prevent,  prepare  for, protect  against,  and respond  to terrorist  attacks
  and other threats  and hazards  that pose the greatest  risk to the security  of the United
  States.

  HSGP  provides  resources  that support  eligible  SLTT  governments;  high-
  density  urban  areas, and SLTT  law enforcement  along  international  land/water
  borders  and travel  corridors  in meeting  the following  objectives:
  *  Build  and sustain  core capabilities,  including  Law  Enforcement  and Terrorism
  Prevention  Activities  and the National  Priority  Areas  (see priorities  below);

SHSP  and  UASI  Funding  Priorities:  Given  the evolving  national  security  threat
landscape,  DHS/FEMA  has evacuated  the national  risk profile  and set priorities  that
help inform  appropriate  allocation  of scarce security  dollars.  In assessing  the national
risk profile  for FY 2024,  six National  Priority  Areas  pose the most concern.  Due to
the unique  threats  that the nation  faces in 2024,  DHS/FEMA  has determined  that
recipients  should  allocate  a total  of 30% of their  SHSP  and UASI  award  funds  across
these six priority  areas. As indicated  below,  one of the priorities  has a minimum
spend requirement  totaling  3% of SHSP and UASI  awards.  Recipients  will  have the
flexibility  to allocate  the remaining  27% across the priorities.  The following  are the
six priority  areas for FY 2024,  along  with  the minimum  corresponding  percentage  of
SHSP  and UASI  funds  that each recipient  will  be required  to allocate:

  l)  Enhancing  the protection  of soft targets/crowded  places  - no minimum
  percent
  2)  Enhancing  information  and intelligence  sharing  and analysis  - no minimum
  percent
  3)  Combating  domestic  violent  extremism  - no minirtum  percent
  4)  Enhancing  cybersecurity  - no minimum  percent
  5)  Enhancing  community  preparedness  and resilience  - no minimum  percent
  6)  Enhancing  election  security  - 3%

Additional  information  about  these priority  areas and how  they relate  to achieving
anti-terrorism  capabilities  is included  in Section  D of this NOFO.  Failure  by a
recipient  to propose  investments  and projects  that align  with  the priority  areas and
spending  requirements  will  result  in a recipient  having  a portion  of their  SHSP  and
UASI  funds  (up to 30%)  placed  on hold  until  they provide  projects  that sufficiently
align  to the National  Priority  Areas,  and total  at least the minimum  percentages  per
National  Priority  Area  (as applicable)  and overall  30% of total  SHSP  and UASI
funds.

A state or high-risk  urban  area must  allocate  the remaining  70% of their  funding  to
addressing  capability  gaps (e.g., building/sustaining  capability  and/or  closing
capability  gaps) identified  through  their  THIRA/SPR  process.

For FY 2024, DHS/FEMA  will  award OPSG funds based on risk and the anticipated
effectiveness  of the proposed  use of grant funds upon completion  of the application  review
process. The FY 2024 0PSG  risk assessment is designed  to identify  the risk to border
security  and to assist with the distribution  of funds for the grant program.  Funding  under
OPSG is distributed  based on the risk to the security  of the border  and the effectiveness  of
the proposed  projects.  Entities  eligible  for 'funding  are the state, local, and tribal  law
enforcement  agencies that are located  along the border  of the United  States. DHS/FEMA  will
make final award determinations  based upon a review  of the anticipated  effectiveness  of the

  For the prirposes  of OPSG, the risk is defined  as the potential  for an adverse oritcome
  assessed as a function of threats, vulnerabilities,  and consequences  associated  with  an
  incident, event, or occurrence.

  Based upon ongoing  intelligence  analysis  and extensive  security  reviews,  DHS/CBP
  continues  to focus the bulk of OPSG funds based upon risk analyses. The risk model used to
  allocate  OPSG funds considers  the potential  risk that certain threats pose to border  security
  and estimates  the relative  risk faced by a given area. In evaluating  risk, DHS/CBP  considers
  intelligence,  situational  awareness,  criminal  trends, and statistical  data specific  to each of the
  border  sectors, and the potential  impacts  that these threats pose to the secuiity  of the border
  area. For vulnerability  and consequence,  DHS/CBP  considers  the expected  impact  and
  consequences  of successfiil  border events occtu-ring  in specific  areas.

  Tmeat and vulnerability  are evaluated  based on specific  operational  data from DHS/CBP.
  Tbreat  components  present in each of the sectors are used to determine  the overall  threat
  score. These components are terrorism,  criminal  aliens, drug trafficking  organizations,  and
  alien smuggling organizations.

  Effectiveness  of the proposed  investments  will be evaluated  based on the recipient's
  investment  strategy,  budget,  collaboration,  and past performance.

  M&A  costs are allowed  by the 2024 DHS  Appropriations  Act.  Recipients  may use a
  maximum  of up to 5% of HSGP  fitnds  awarded  for their  M&A,  and any funds
  retained  are to be used solely  for M&A  purposes  associated  with  the HSGP  award.
  Subrecipients  may also use a maximum  of rip to 5% of the funding  passed throrigh  by
  the state solely  for M&A  purposes  associated  with  the HSGP  award.  M&A  activities
  are those directly  relating  to the management  and administation  of HSGP  funds,  such
  as financial  management  and monitoring.  M&A  expenses  must be based on actual
  expenses  or known  contractual  costs. M&A  requests  that are simple  percentages  of
  the award,  without  supporting  justification,  will  not be allowed  or considered  for
  reimbursement.

  M&A  costs are not operational  costs but are necessary  costs incurred  in direct  support
  of the federal  award  or as a consequence  of it, such as travel,  meeting-related
  expenses,  and salaries  of fiill/part-time  staff in direct  support  of the program.  As such,
  M&A  costs can be itemized  in financial  reports.  Otlier  M&A  cost examples  iiiclude
  preparing  and submitting  required  programmatic  and financial  reports,  establishing
  and/or  maintaining  equipment  inventory,  documenting  operational  and equipment
  expenditures  for financial  accounting  purposes,  responding  to official  informational
  requests  from  state and federal  oversiglit  arithorities,  including  completing  the Civil
  Rights  Evaluation  Tool  as required  by DHS,  and grant performance  measurement  or
  evatuation  activities.

  Recipients  or subrecipients  may apply  or credit  M&A  funding  toward  the recipient's
  requirement  to allocate  funding  toward  the National  Priority  Areas.  For example,  if a
  recipient  spends  $5,000  to manage  or administer  its funding  dedicated  toward  its
  election  security  investment,  the recipient  may credit  that funding  toward  its
  requirement  to allocate  at least 3% of its award  to the enhancing  election  security
  National  Priority  Area.

  While  the SAA  may retain  up to 5% of HSGP  funds  awarded  for M&A,  the state
  must  still  ensure that all subrecipient  award  amounts  meet the mandatory  minimum
  pass-throrigh  reqriirements  that are applicable  to each HSGP  program.  To meet this

  r.  RISK METHODOLOGY
  The risk methodology  determines  the relative  risk of terrorism  faced  by a given
  area considering  the potential  risk  of terrorism  to people,  critical  infrastruchire,
  and economic  security.  The analysis  includes,  but is not limited  to, threats  from
  violent  domestic  extremists,  international  terrorist  grorips,  individuals  inspired  by
  terrorists  abroad,  and the assessment  of vulnerabilities  and potential
  conseqriences.  DHS  defines  risk as: "potential  for an adverse  outcome  assessed as
  a function  of hazard/threats,  assets and their  vulnerabilities,  and consequences  "
  See DHS  Lexicon  Terms  and Definitions:  2018  Edition  - Revision  04, (Apr.
  2018).  The FEMA  risk methodology  is focused  on three elements:
  i.  Threat:  the likelihood  of an attack  being  attempted  by an adversary;
  ii.  Vulnerability:  the likelihood  that an attack  is successful,  given  that
  it is attempted;  and
  iii.  Consequence:  the effect  of an event,  incident,  or occurrence.

  NOTE:  The THIRA/SPR  process  is separate  from  the risk methodology  and its
  results  do not affect  grant  allocations.

  The Risk  Methodology  is used to infortn  allocations  under  HSGP.  For more

2.  Pass-Through  Requirements
  Awards  made to the SAA for HSGP carry additional  statutorily  mandated  pass-through
  requirements.  Pass-tbrorigh  is defined  as an obligation  on the part of the SAA to make funds
  available  to local units of government,  combinations  of local units, tribal  governments,  or
  other specific  groups or organizations.  Tliese entities  are defined  at 6 u.s.c. § 101(13)  as:
  *  A county,  municipality,  city, town, township,  local public  authority,  school  district,
  special  district,  intrastate  district,  council  of governments  (regardless  of whether  the
  council  of governments  is incorporated  as a nonprofit  corporation  under State law),
  regional or interstate  government  entity,  or agency or insti'umentality  of a local
  government.
  *  An Indian  tribe or authorized  tribal  organization,  or in Alaska  a Native  village  or
  Alaska  Regional  Native  Corporation.
  *  A rural community,  unincorporated  town or village,  or other public  entity.

  Four  criteria  must  be met to pass-through  grant  funds:
  *  The SAA must make a firm written  commitment  to passing through  grant funds to
  subrecipients;
  *  The SAA's  commitment  must be unconditional  (i.e., no contingencies  for the
  availability  of SAA  funds);
  *  There must be documentary  evidence  (i.e., award document,  terms, and conditions)
  of the commitment; and
  *  The award terms must be comtmuiicated  to the subrecipient.

  Timing  and Amount
  The SAA must pass-through  at least 80% of the funds awarded under SHSP and UASI  to the
  above-defined  local or tribal  units of government  within  45 calendar  days of receipt  of the
  funds. "Receipt  of the funds"  occurs either when the SAA accepts the award or 15 calendar
  days after the SAA receives  notice of the award, wliichever  is earlier.

  SAAs  are sent notification  of HSGP awards via the FEMA  GO system. If an SAA  accepts its
  award within  15 calendar  days of receiving  notice  of the award in the FEMA  GO system, the
  45 calendar  days pass-through  period  will  start on the date the SAA  accepted the award.

8. Notes  on  Personnel  Cost:

In qeneral,  costs  associated  with:

€ Work performed  under contract  for a specific  deliverable  DOES  NOT count  against  the
  personnel cap, however,
€ Work  performed  under contract  for an undefined  period,  such as for personnel  costs
  supporting  operational  activities,  including  general  planning,  training  or exercise
  activities  DO count  against  the personnel  cap; and
€ Work  performed  by all non-contractor  personnel,  including  for full- or part-time  staff and
  operational  overtime  DO count  against  the personnel  cap.

The followinq  examples  would  not count  towards  the personnel  cap:

€ Vendor  installation  of a radio tower;
€ Vendor  training  on new equipment  purchased
€ Contractor  hired to create  an Emergency  Operations  Plan
€ Contractor  hired to provide  deliveries  of ICS 400; and
€ Contractor  hired to assist with planning,  training,  evaluating,  and reporting  the
  effectiveness  of a specific  exercise.

The followinq  examples  would  count  towards  the personnel  cap:
€ Contractor  hired to be the State's  WMD  training  instructor  with no specific  deliverables
  under contract;
€ Contractor  hired to facilitate  unidentified  number  of exercises  throughout  the
  performance  period;
€ Contractor  hired to be the part-time  auditor  of Homeland  Security  Grants  throughout  the year; and
€ Contractor  hired to be an intelligence  analyst.

BACKGROUND:  The City's  roadway  network  relies  on a limited  number  of major  streets that
cross over the Interstate  710 Freeway  and the Los Angeles  River.  These  crossings  are critical  for
moving  people  and traffic  across  the City.  Historically,  Southern  Avenue  also provided  this
connection;  however,  the bridge  was removed  following  an emergency  event.  This created  a gap
in the roadway  network,  which  continues  to place  additional  traffic  pressure  on nearby  crossings
such as Firestone  Boulevard  and Imperial  Highway.  As a result,  congestion  in this area remains  a
challenge  due to the limited  number  of available  bridges.

The Southeni  Avenue  Multimodal  Bridge  Project  is intended  to address  this long-standing  issue
by restoring  this connection.  The project  proposes  to construct  a new bridge  that would  reconnect
Garfield  Avenue  to Atlantic  Avenue,  via  Southern  Avenue.  In  addition  to improving  traffic
circulation,  the project  is designed  to enhance  safety  and access for pedestrians,  bicyclists,  and
transit  users.  It would  also strengthen  connections  between  neighborhoods,  Urban  Orchard  Park,
the Los Angeles  River  corridor,  and fiiture  development  areas.

The City  received  a $500,000  Measure  A Grant  from  the Los Angeles  County  Regional  Park and
Open Space District  to study the feasibility  of constructing  the new bridge.  This funding  is limited
to planning  and preliminary  design  and does not include  construction.  The  study  will  evaluate
whether  the project  can be built  and what it would  require.  Key tasks include:

  *  Developing  and comparing  bridge  design  options

  @  Evaluating  environmental  constraints

  *  Analyzing  traffic,  roadway  connections,  and right-of-way  needs

  *  Conducting  bilingual  community  outreach

  Preparing  a final  report  with  cost estimates  and a long-term  project  schedule

The planning  phase  is expected  to take approximately  two  years,  from  July  2026  through  June
2028.

  mitigation  plan  The Southern Avenue Multimodal Bridge Planning Study area includes multiple
  agencies, flood control facilities, and transportation infrastructure that are known
  site constraints typical of a regional multimodal bridge project each introducing
  technical, environmental,  and permitting complexity. The corridor's mix of
  infrastructure  and land uses requires careful integration. These issues are
  incorporated into the planning scope so they can be evaluated, mitigated, and
  turned into opportunities for stronger connectivity, community access, and land-
  use coordination.

  Land Use and Corridor Function
  The bridge will connect three fragmented sections of Southern Avenue now
  divided by the 1-710 Freeway and Los Angeles River. It will create a new east-
  west community connections for bicycle, pedestrian, and transit services
  providing safe non-motorized  connections to residential areas, South Gate Park
  and Llrban Orchard Park, two regional bike trails, future light-rail station,
  employment centers, and local/regional community services. The route follows
  Southern Avenue where adjacent parcels include older industrial sites. Several
  parcels identified by the Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) for
  remediation could include redevelopment  support housing, recreation or retail
  consistent with the LA River Master Plan and the planned multimodal design of
  the bridge.

  Multi-Jurisdictional  Coordination
  Implementation  will require partnership with Caltrans District 7 and the LA County
  Flood Control District. A Project Partnering Group and letters of intent will clarify
  responsibilities,  share data, and outline permits. Additional stakeholders
  including utilities, LA Metro, and others will be invited to participate as the project
  planning proceeds.

  Utilities and Infrastructure
  Existing utilities - power, communications,  and storm drains - will be identified
  through record research and coordination  with owners. Bridge alternatives will
  integrate avoidance, relocation strategies,  and may consider new
  technology/green  infrastructure mitigation  strategies.

  Topography, Flood Control, and Hydraulics
  The bridge must span the river channel while maintaining clearance and flow
  capacity. The area's flat grades require precise geometry. Screening-level
  hydraulic modeling and coordination with Flood Control will confirm elevations
  and pier placement, offering opportunities for aesthetic and habitat-sensitive
  design consistent with LA River Master Plan goals.

  Environmental  and Contamination Constraints
  Given the urban setting and freeway proximity, legacy soil or air-quality concerns
  may exist. The study will perform environmental  constraints screening to identify
  risks and inform future CEQA/NEPA steps while highlighting opportunities to
  reduce Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) and improve air quality through expanded
  active-transportation  options.

  Right-of-Way and Access
  The bridge alignment lies within City-owned right-or-way extending across the
  freeway, river, and adjoining parcels, with partial connections on property
  managed by Caltrans and LA County Flood Control. The study will map
  ownership of impacted parcels. Draft cooperative-use  language for future

  554
   agreements  defining  access  and maintenance  roles will be prepared  as needed.

  Structural  and Design Feasibility
  Long spans are required to cross both the freeway and river while meeting
  seismic and multimodal  standards.  The Measure A-funded  analysis will identify
  feasible  bridge types, materials,  and construction  methods,  creating opportunities
  for integrated  architectural  and landscape  design that enhance visibility, safety,
  and community  identity.

  Public Access, Safety, and Placemaking
  The bridge will link roadways,  sidewalks,  bikeways,  and bus routes through ADA-
  compliant  connections.  The study will evaluate tie-ins, visibility, and bicycle
  approaches.  Bilingual community  (English/Spanish)  engagement  will include

  Gate's cultural and environmental  context and align with the LA River Master

(Name and describe role(s))
  The Southern Avenue Multimodal  Bridge Planning  Study will be delivered through
  strong partnerships  among public agencies,  community  organizations,  and
  technical  stakeholders.  Because the project crosses the 1-710 Freeway and the
  Los Angeles  River, long-term  success depends  on sustained  coordination  with
  the agencies that own and manage the right-of-way,  along with those
  representing  the surrounding  community.  The partnership  framework  outlined
  below ensures consistent  communication,  shared decision-making,  and
  transparent  progress throughout  the planning phase.

  Primary Agency Partners
  Caltrans District 7 and the Los Angeles  County Flood Control District are the
  project's two primary partner agencies.  Both own and manage portions of the
  right-of-way  where the future bridge will cross the freeway and river. Their roles
  include providing  data, design and hydraulic  criteria, and early review of technical
  studies to confirm feasibility  and regulatory  consistency.  Letters of intent will
  document  each agency's  consent to participate  in planning activities and
  establish the foundation  for future cooperative  agreements  or permits. Each
  partner will be represented  in a Project Partnering  Group convened  by the City of
  South Gate at key milestones  to review alternatives,  evaluate environmental  and

  557
   access  considerations,  and confirm  constructability.

  Regional Transportation  Partner
  LA Metro will serve as a planning partner through its Transit Planning and Joint
  Development  teams. Metro's participation  will help align the bridge concepts with
  the regional bus network,  planned Light Rail Transit corridor, and potential
  Transit-Oriented  Development  (TOD) opportunities.  Early collaboration  with Metro
  will ensure that the Southern Avenue corridor strengthens  ffrsUlast-mile
  connectivity  and supports  equitable  transit access.

  Local Government  and Inter-City  Coordination
  The City of South Gate Public Works Department  is the lead agency responsible
  for overall project management,  consultant  oversight,  and grant fiscal reporting.
  City departments  staff including  Parks and Recreation,  Community  Development,
  and Police and Fire Services will contribute  to planning, access design, safety
  review, and public outreach.  Coordination  will also extend to City oT Downey staff,
  given the project's proximity to the municipal boundary  and shared transportation
  network. This partnership  ensures that regional connectivity  and emergency-
  response  access are fully addressed  in the bridge concepts.

  Educational  and Institutional  Stakeholders
  The planning study will coordinate  with the Los Angeles Unified School District
  (LAUSD)  and local school principals to ensure that student routes and pedestrian
  safety needs are reflected  in design concepts.  Early input from school
  representatives  will support identification  of preferred crossings,  travel routes,
  and community  engagement  strategies  during the public workshop.

  Community  and Economic  Stakeholders
  Engagement  will include local businesses,  property owners, and community-
  based organizations  (CBOs) active near Southern Avenue and the Los Angeles
  River. Their participation  will help identify potential access improvements,
  aesthetic  treatments,  and cultural design features such as public art or
  interpretive  elements.  Outreach  will prioritize equity and bilingual communication
  to ensure that residents  most affected by the project are fully represented  in
  decisions.

  Partner Coordination  and Deliverables
  Under Task 3.2 - Stakeholder  List and Coordination,  the consultant  team, working
  with the city, will develop and maintain a detailed contact list identifying  each
  partner's  point of contact and role. The list will be used to distribute  notices, share
  draft deliverables,  and document  feedback during each project phase.
  Coordination  will occur through virtual or in-person  meetings,  technical  reviews,
  and public engagement  sessions.

  This partnership  structure  builds on the City's long history of collaboration  with
  regional and community  organizations.  It provides a transparent  framework  for
  input, regulatory  coordination,  and inter-agency  problem-solving.  Through this
  collective  effort, the planning study will produce bridge concepts  that are
  technically  feasible,  environmentally  responsible,  and publicly supported,  which
  positions the City of South Gate and its partners to advance a multimodal  east-
  west gateway  project that improves  safety, mobility, and access to the Los
  Angeles  River corridor.

 Describe your project delivery
approach.  The City of South Gate will serve as the lead agency and contract administrator
  for the Southern Avenue Multimodal  Bridge Planning Study. The City has
  extensive  experience managing  consultant-led  planning and design projects
  funded through local, state, and federal programs.

  The project will be delivered  through a consultant  services agreement  managed
  by the Public Works Department,  consistent  with the City's adopted Public Works
  procurement  procedures  and the California  Public Contract  Code. All services will
  be competitively  solicited through a Request for Proposals  (RFP) process to
  ensure transparency,  cost control, and qualifications-based  selection. The City
  will issue the RFP, evaluate proposals,  and recommend  award to the City Council
  for authorization.

  Once a consultant  team is under contract, the City will provide overall project
  management,  contract administration,  and coordination  with Regional Park and
  Open Space District (RPOSD)  and partner agencies.  A designated  City Project
  Manager  (City Engineer  or designee)  will serve as the primary point of contact,
  responsible  for schedule  oversight,  budget monitoring,  and task approvals.  City
  staff will review deliverables,  coordinate  internal and interagency  comments,  and
  approve invoices before submittal to RPOSD.

  The selected  consultant  team will be responsible  for all technical  and
  engagement  tasks outlined in the Measure A funded scope, including feasibility
  analysis,  development  of bridge concepts and alternatives,  environmental
  constraints  mapping,  and bilingual community  engagement.  Technical specialists
  will prepare structural  and hydrology  screening,  access evaluations,  and a
  Planning and Environmental  Linkages (PEL) outline identifying  the CEQA/NEPA
  pathway for future phases. All work products will be reviewed  and approved  by
  City staff prior to submittal.

  A Project Steering Group will be established  to ensure coordinated  review and
  progress  monitoring.  This group will include representatives  from the City of
  South Gate, Caltrans District 7, Los Angeles County Flood Control District, LA
  Metro, and the Rivers and Mountains  Conservancy,  reflecting  the project's multi-
  jurisdictional  setting. The Steering Group will convene at key milestones  to review
  technical  findings,  evaluate bridge alternatives,  and ensure consistency  with
  agency standards  and future permitting  requirements.

  Community  engagement  will be fully integrated  into the project delivery process.
  The consultant  team, with City oversight, will lead three bilingual public workshop
  and up to three stakeholder  meetings  to gather feedback  on bridge concepts  and
  river access alternatives.  Meeting logistics, translation,  and outreach materials
  will be coordinated  by City staff. Public feedback  will be documented  and
  incorporated  into the feasibility  findings and final recommendations.

  Quality assurance  and quality control (QA/QC) will be implemented  throughout
  the project. Each technical  deliverable  will undergo internal review by the
  consultant  team, followed  by City and partner agency review to ensure technical
  accuracy,  regulatory  consistency,  and alignment  with Measure A objectives.

  Financial  management  will adhere to RPOSD's  Grant Administration  Manual
  (GAM) and City of South Gate accounting  policies. The City will maintain clear
  documentation  of expenditures,  staff time, and consultant  invoices, and will
  submit quarterly  progress  reports and reimbursement  requests through RPOSD's
  Grant Management  System.
